analysis.title: AI's Path to $2 Trillion in Revenue
key_insights: Apollo estimates cumulative AI infrastructure capex across hyperscalers, chipmakers, model developers and neocloud providers could reach about $3.5 trillion through 2028, based on announced plans.
Demand for compute still exceeds supply, GPU rental prices are rising, and some infrastructure providers report capital payback periods under one year.

Apollo estimates AI needs about $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion of annualized revenue by end-2028 to justify the buildout, roughly 5-7 times today's level. By 2030 the figure could reach $3 trillion to $5 trillion, depending on how much more infrastructure is deployed.

Unit economics: each GW of AI compute costs about $7 billion a year to run (depreciation plus opex), and with a margin stacked at the infrastructure, model builder and app layers, needs about $20 billion of annual end-user revenue. Deployed capacity of about 100 GW by end-2028 gives the $1.5-$2 trillion requirement.

Annualized AI application revenue was about $200 billion in Q2 2026, up from $11 billion in early 2024, and about $276 billion by September 2026, roughly 3.75-fold annual growth since 2023. The estimate excludes AI-driven ad uplift at Google and Meta and chip sales.

Reaching $1.5-$2 trillion by end-2028 requires AI revenue to grow about 2.3 to 2.6 times a year for two years. Apollo says recent growth rates make this achievable, but growth gets harder as the base expands.
Deployment risks: power constraints, chip shortages, construction delays and restrictive policy after the midterms could slow the buildout.

Capital markets act as a check. If AI revenue disappoints, lower valuations and higher financing costs would slow spending and reduce the revenue needed. Anthropic's S-1 warns slower revenue growth could constrain compute investment and weigh on capex plans for the second half of 2027 and 2028.

Spending is flexible: Anthropic describes deferring larger accelerator investments until compute needs are more certain. Most of the cost sits in accelerators and IT equipment that can be deferred, though contractual commitments already made remain.
More vertical integration or ecosystem subsidies would lower the revenue needed, because the model stacks a margin at each of three layers.

Size comparison: the $1.5-$2 trillion target exceeds global enterprise software (about $1.2 trillion), and compares with semiconductors ($795 billion), online advertising ($715 billion) and cloud ($419 billion). Global labor income is about $58 trillion.

Demand sources: the median enterprise puts about 7% of its IT budget into AI against about 23% for AI-native organizations (McKinsey, May 2026). Consumer subscriptions and advertising budgets, and expansion into pharma, cybersecurity and defense, are other sources.

Apollo's view is that the open question is whether revenue grows fast enough to support the buildout, not whether AI can reach scale. Phased capacity builds and deferrable accelerator spend limit the downside.

sector_views.rationale: Apollo expects AI revenue to keep rising rapidly, but the buildout needs 2.3-2.6x annual revenue growth through 2028 and depends on deployment staying on schedule.

risk_factors: Power constraints, chip shortages and construction delays could slow AI infrastructure deployment.
Restrictive policies after the midterms could slow deployment.
AI revenue disappointing would raise financing costs and lower valuations, which could cut capex for the second half of 2027 and 2028.
Growth becomes harder to sustain as the AI revenue base expands.
Vera Rubin chips would carry higher annual depreciation and opex, closer to $9bn per GW, raising the revenue required per GW.
Contractual obligations on capacity already committed remain even if the buildout slows.
charts_described: Exhibit 1 breaks the $20B per GW revenue requirement into depreciation plus opex of $6.8B, infrastructure margin of $3.7B, model builder margin of $5.3B and app margin of $3.9B, giving $11B infrastructure, $16B model builder and $20B app revenue per GW.
Exhibit 2 shows the AI revenue run rate path to about $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion by end-2028, at 2.3x and 2.6x annual growth.
geopolitical: Restrictive policies in the aftermath of the midterms are cited as a risk that could slow AI infrastructure deployment.

tension_points.bull_case: Compute demand exceeds supply, GPU rental prices are rising, some providers report payback under a year, and application revenue has grown about 3.75x a year, so the 2.3-2.6x annual growth needed looks achievable.
tension_points.bear_case: Growth gets harder as the base expands, deployment could be slowed by power, chips, construction and policy, and slower revenue could cut capex for the second half of 2027 and 2028 as Anthropic's S-1 warns.
tension_points.what_invalidates: AI revenue growth falling short of the 2.3-2.6x annual pace needed to reach $1.5-$2 trillion by end-2028, which would raise financing costs and slow capex in the second half of 2027 and 2028.

theme_stances.key_argument: AI revenue will likely keep rising rapidly as it reaches more use cases, and the buildout can adjust because most cost sits in deferrable accelerators and IT equipment.
theme_stances.evidence: AI revenue will likely continue to increase rapidly over the next few years
